rules.topic: Can a tenancy require (or charge for) a professional clean? (Tenant Fees Act 2019)
rules.verdict: No. A landlord/agent cannot require the tenant to pay for a professional clean or use a particular cleaning company; they may only ask that it is returned in the condition found (they may request a professional standard).
rules.quote: Q. Can I charge a tenant for a professional clean at the end of a tenancy? No. You cannot require a tenant to pay for a professional clean when they check-out. ... You cannot require a tenant to use a particular company to clean the property. ... You cannot require a tenant to meet any conditions that could only be met by paying a fee for a third-party service (e.g. requiring a professional clean at the end of the tenancy).
rules.caveat: This GOV.UK guidance PDF carries a 'Withdrawn' watermark (search snippet: withdrawn 8 May 2026) and is superseded by guidance updated for the Renters' Rights Act 2025; the current GOV.UK pages fetched did not restate the cleaning wording, but cleaning remains outside the Act's permitted payments.

rules.topic: Can the landlord deduct cleaning costs from the deposit, limited to restoring move-in condition (fair wear and tear excluded)?
rules.verdict: Yes, but only the evidenced cost of returning the property to its move-in condition; no deduction for fair wear and tear or if returned as found.
rules.quote: Tenants are responsible for ensuring that the property is returned in the condition that they found it, aside from any fair wear and tear. ... If the property is not left in a fit condition, you can recover costs associated with returning the property to its original condition and/or carrying out necessary repairs by claiming against the tenancy deposit. You should justify your costs by providing suitable evidence (e.g. an independently produced inventory, receipts and invoices). You are not able to claim deductions from a tenant's deposit for any change in the condition of the property which is due to fair wear and tear or if a tenant returns the property in the same condition as it was found.

rules.topic: Deductions must be reasonable; tenant need not pay for professional cleaning (Shelter)
rules.verdict: Professional cleaning is optional; deductions must be reasonable and reflect landlord's actual loss; no deduction for fair wear and tear.
rules.quote: Some renters choose to pay for professional cleaning before they move out to avoid disputes over the deposit but you do not have to do this. ... Your landlord cannot keep any of your deposit for 'fair wear and tear'. ... Any deposit deductions must be reasonable and relate to money lost by the landlord.

rules.topic: Cleaning standard = move-in standard; claims proportionate (mydeposits scheme)
rules.verdict: Tenant only has to match the check-in cleanliness; landlord can't claim a full clean where not needed. Note fair wear and tear does not excuse dirt.
rules.quote: The tenant is only responsible for returning the property cleaned to the same standard it was in at the start. ... Costs claimed by the landlord must be proportionate to the breach and not for a full clean where it is not required. ... Fair wear and tear only applies to condition and does not extend to cleaning.

rules.topic: Landlord must evidence deductions (current statutory guidance, Renters' Rights Act update)
rules.verdict: Landlord/agent must provide evidence for any deposit deduction.
rules.quote: a landlord or agent will need to provide evidence to support any deductions from the deposit at the end of the tenancy.

rules.topic: How common are cleaning deposit disputes? (TDS 2024/25)
rules.verdict: Cleaning is the #1 dispute cause: in 54% of TDS adjudicated disputes in 2024/25 (damage 49%), though only ~1% of deposits go to adjudication.
rules.quote: Cleaning continues to be the single biggest source of disputes, appearing in over half of all TDS dispute cases. ... In the 12 months to March 2025, just 1% of all deposits (46,950 cases) required formal adjudication.
Cleaning remains the most frequent trigger for disagreements, featuring in 54% of cases.
